history.content: What is Cassava brown streak virus and how can I manage it?

history.content: why sorghum stays stunted yellow

draws.answer: Stunting from yellowing is caused by a nitrogen shortage from depleted organic matter. First, do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK compound or a systemic fungicide, because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on run-down soil. Second, bring organic matter back by applying manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Third, rotate with a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Fourth, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper fertilizer dose for your plot before any large purchase. ICAT is the service to see.

The yellowing starts on the old lower leaves and gets worse each season, and the plants cannot be greener each year. Stunted plants grow at a reduced height, often with a uniform pale yellowing of the older leaves, while the younger leaves stay greener. This pattern is typical of nitrogen shortage from depleted soil. To restore yellowing, bring back organic matter with manure, compost, or unburnt residues. Avoid selling the old stalks and keep the residues in the soil. Then plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. For a soil test and the correct fertilizer dose, see ICAT.

history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: No, you cannot mix insecticides because the Togolese service does not allow it. What the service will not give you is the strength of the mix and the rate, and that is information you would have to get from ICAT. What you can do safely is check the label on the approved product, look for a product that is marked insecticide and read the label before you spray, and wear gloves and a gas mask when you open the container.

history.content: My goats have a mucky discharge from their eyes and some are dying quickly. What steps must I take?

draws.answer: Those signs point to leucaena poisoning caused by excessive leucaena in the diet. Blend the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to provide plenty of roughage for the rumen. Change the feed composition gradually over several days. Keep clean water and a mineral or salt source always available. If the goats keep refusing food, keep drooling or develop a swollen throat, see the veterinary service.

history.content: how far should fields be spaced to avoid spread

draws.answer: Spacing depends on the crop and the practice, but you should keep the field edge clear of weeds that host the pests. For example, maize is sown in rows spaced 80 cm apart, which is one row of 40 cm, two rows of 20 cm, or a pocket of 20 cm within the row for extra early varieties. In the north, Maritime and Plateaux, use a staggered system with 2 m between rows and 1.5 m between pockets. In the south, Kara and Savanes, use a single line with 2 m between rows and 1.5 m between pockets. For the reasons behind the spacing, see ICAT.

The spacing depends on the crop and the rotation. history.content: What steps should I take to manage Striga hermonthica in my sorghum crop?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that attaches itself to your sorghum and prevents the plant from developing proper roots. First, sow your sorghum at a spacing of 60-65 cm per pocket and place seeds in rows spaced 80 cm. Wait about two weeks after sowing to transplant the seedlings into the field. Then perform the first weeding of the sorghum about one week after transplanting. At about 30-35 days after transplant, treat the plants by dropping a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel; one kilogram will cover roughly 1,500-2,000 plants and you should repeat this every eight to ten days. Never apply neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the sorghum. After the sorghum is harvested, cut the stems at ground level and leave the nodules in the soil to fix nitrogen for the next crop. If a large block is heavily infested, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that attaches to sorghum and takes its nitrogen. First, perform the striga break at 2-3 weeks after sowing by using a striga-tolerant sorghum variety. Next, pull out any remaining Striga plants from the field. Then, rotate or intercrop the land with a legume such as cowpea or soybean to remove the parasitic plant from the soil. history.content: My sorghum has Striga, it must be nutrient deficiency, so I just add fertilizer

draws.answer: It is not Striga, it is nitrogen depletion of the soil. Striga is a parasitic plant that takes root in the soil while the sorghum grows, and it is not a deficiency that shows up after fertiliser. To tell them apart, look at the leaves: in a nitrogen shortage the older lower leaves stay green while the young top leaves become pale and drop, and the plant may become short with these leaves. Because it is nitrogen depletion, you need to restore organic matter first, then add a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. After that, apply a NPK 20-20-20 at 150 kg per hectare at panicle initiation, then keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you have soil that has been exhausted, see ICAT for a soil analysis before buying any mineral fertilizer.

draws.answer: You have cassava bacterial blight. Remove and destroy the affected plants right away. Disinfect your tools between each plant to avoid spreading the bacterium. Ask an ITRA representative to confirm the diagnosis and to give you clean resistant cuttings.

Get clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer and ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.

history.content: When I harvest, the cassava roots are brown and corky, what caused that and how can I prevent it next season?

draws.answer: You said the cassava roots are brown and corky after harvesting and you are wondering what caused it and how to stop it for the next season. I have to tell you this problem is not something I was taught, and I will not guess a cause, a pest, a disease, a product or a dose because that could mislead you. Look at the cassava plants closely and note what you see - which leaves or parts are affected, whether the damage started in one spot or throughout, if it follows the rows, low ground or field edge, and whether it appeared after rain, a dry spell or any treatment. Pull one affected plant with its roots, keep it in a bag with a few leaves, and do not spray anything until someone has seen it. Take the sample and your notes to the ICAT extension agent, who can look at the field.

Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen gets enough roughage. Change the feed composition slowly over several days. history.content: My sorghum is very short and the base has a pinkish weed that looks like it is holding on tightly. How can I manage this problem?

draws.answer: The short sorghum and pinkish weed indicate stalk borer or aphid feeding. While the plants are still young, place a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel; one kilogram treats about 1,500-2,000 plants. Repeat the pinch every 8-10 days as long as the young plants are still young. Never apply neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant. After harvesting, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large block is attacked, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

history.content: My cassava leaves have yellow streaks on the veins and when I dig up the roots they are brown and corky. What should I do?

draws.answer: Those signs are cassava brown streak disease. Pull out the strongly corky and twisted cassava roots from those plants and destroy them. Clean your cutting tools before you work on another plant to avoid spread. After that, select cuttings only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no yellow or pale streaks, never from a damaged stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. For clean tolerant cuttings you should see ITRA.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that attaches itself to your sorghum and takes its nutrients. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five grains per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Do not grow sorghum after maize because the root system competes with it. Two to three weeks after sowing, perform the first weeding of your field. Then apply the three flowering-stage sprays to protect the sorghum panicles. For variety selection that matches your region and season, consult ICAT.
